title: Overflow

9.name: Buffer Overflow
9.vuln: Can be exploited to cause unexpected behavior, useful for many attack vectors.

18.name: Format String Vulnerability
18.vuln: Allows leaking stack data or writing to memory via format specifiers.

title: Kernel

18.name: Integer Underflow
18.vuln: If 'len' is 0, 'len - 1' wraps to the maximum value of size_t, bypassing the bounds check entirely.

22.name: Heap/Mmap Buffer Overflow
22.vuln: Reading 'len + 16' bytes into a buffer of size 'len' allows overwriting adjacent memory metadata or mapped structures.

29.name: Use-After-Free (UAF)
29.vuln: The 'session' object is freed on a specific 'req_type' but the callback is still invoked, allowing an attacker to hijack the instruction pointer (EIP/RIP) if they can reclaim that heap chunk.

title: Ion-Vault

11.name: Heap Determinism / Uninitialized Memory
11.vuln: The malloc'd 'cfg' struct is never initialized. In certain glibc versions or thread-local caches, this chunk may contain stale data from previous allocations (like 'secret_key'), allowing an attacker to influence the 'priority' check.

16.name: Stack-Based Off-By-One Buffer Overflow
16.vuln: The loop condition 'i <= sizeof(dest)' allows writing one byte past the end of 'dest'. On many architectures, this overwrites the least significant byte of the saved frame pointer or an adjacent local variable, leading to control flow hijacking.

21.name: Arbitrary Command Execution (Privilege Escalation)
21.vuln: The 'system' call uses a hardcoded path but relies on the environment. If the PATH variable is not sanitized or the binary is SUID, an attacker can manipulate the environment to trigger unauthorized file access.

title: Denial

42.name: Unconditional execution leading to DOS
42.vuln: It fails to check if a timeout occured (time_diff <=0) this causes the system to immediately identify the first connection it finds as timed out and terminates it leading to a DOS

43.name: Logic Bypass / Control Flow Hijack
43.vuln: The unconditional break statement prevents the execution of expiration tracking (Line 44) and forces a loop exit. This allows an attacker to bypass legitimate timeout logic and trigger immediate, unintended connection termination.

title: Global Failure

1.name: Assert-Only State Validation
1.vuln: The code uses 'passert' (likely a production-removable assertion) to check if globals are reset. If assertions are disabled in production builds, the check is skipped entirely, allowing the function to run with 'dirty' state from a previous request.

4.name: Resource Cleanup Bypass / State Leak
4.vuln: The function returns 'v2N_INVALID_KE_PAYLOAD' immediately without calling 'reset_globals()'. This leaves the global state modified or 'dirty' for the next packet processor, leading to potential cross-session data leakage or logic corruption.

7.name: Delayed State Reset
7.vuln: Global state is only reset at line 7, but lines 1-6 have already performed assertions and logical operations. This creates a race window or logic gap where the code relies on state that hasn't been explicitly cleared yet.

title: Responder

5.name: Side-Channel Information Leakage
5.vuln: The immediate error assignment establishes an observable state change that leaks critical metadata regarding the internal state of the decryption process

6.name: Non-constant Time Early Exit
6.vuln: Aborting the process early allows attackers to use timing analysis between padding errors and MAC failures, eventually decrypting to plaintext

title: null

5.name: Null Pointer Dereference (Out-of-Bounds Access)
5.vuln: The loop condition checks for a next image, but the logic at line 5 immediately calls GetNextImageInList(p) and dereferences it without verifying the pointer. A red teamer can provide a crafted image sequence to trigger a crash (DoS) or potentially exploit the memory corruption state.
